The core mechanism of behavioral oscillation arises from the interplay between conditioned stimulus components and novel intrusions. The system exhibits a dual nature: it maintains stability under consistent conditions but oscillates when new stimulus elements are introduced. This behavior can be modeled as a stochastic process where the mean response shifts according to the variance of the stimulus components. The afferent impulse modulation introduces a dynamic element that alters the neural signal strength, leading to measurable changes in response amplitude. When a novel stimulus component enters the system, it modifies the afferent input, causing a reduction in the overall reaction strength—this is captured by the damping function. These interactions form a closed-loop system where each perturbation influences subsequent responses, creating oscillatory patterns. The mathematical framework integrates these phenomena through probabilistic mappings of stimulus variance to response variability, enabling prediction of oscillation characteristics.
